title: Calling REST APIs
summary: Invoke-RestMethod and Invoke-WebRequest with headers, bearer tokens and JSON bodies; pagination done right; retries, timeouts and status codes.

steps.title: Invoke-RestMethod: JSON in, objects out
body: `Invoke-RestMethod` (alias `irm`) sends an HTTP request and **converts a JSON (or XML) response into objects**, so
the result goes straight into the pipeline:
```powershell
$token = Get-Secret -Name OpsApiToken -AsPlainText           # module 7; here: a file only you can read
$headers = @{ Authorization = "Bearer $token"; Accept = 'application/json' }
$page = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'https://api.example.com/v1/tickets?page=1' -Headers $headers
$page.items | Where-Object priority -eq 'urgent'
$body = @{ title = 'Disk full on fs02'; priority = 'high' } | ConvertTo-Json
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri 'https://api.example.com/v1/tickets' -Headers $headers -Body $body -ContentType 'application/json'
`Invoke-WebRequest` (`iwr`) returns the raw response instead: `.StatusCode`, `.Headers`, `.Content`. Use it when you
need headers or the bytes (downloads with `-OutFile`).
Switches that matter in automation (PowerShell 7):
| Switch | Does |
| `-TimeoutSec 10` | give up instead of hanging the job (the default waits a very long time) |
| `-MaximumRetryCount 3 -RetryIntervalSec 2` | retry failed requests (5xx, 429, ...) by itself |
| `-SkipHttpErrorCheck` | do not throw on 4xx/5xx; look at the status yourself |
| `-StatusCodeVariable sc` | put the HTTP status code in `$sc` |
| `-Authentication Bearer -Token $secureToken` | send a token from a `SecureString` (HTTPS only, unless `-AllowUnencryptedAuthentication`) |

steps.prompt: You need the `ETag` response header of a REST call and its status code, as well as the body. Which command gives you all three most directly?
options: `Invoke-RestMethod`: it returns only the converted body by default
steps.explain: `Invoke-RestMethod` is the right default because it gives you objects, but it hides the response. `Invoke-WebRequest` keeps everything (then `$r.Content | ConvertFrom-Json` for the body). In PowerShell 7, `Invoke-RestMethod -ResponseHeadersVariable h -StatusCodeVariable s` is the middle way.

steps.title: Pagination: an API rarely returns everything
body: Most APIs return a **page** (20, 50, 100 items) and tell you where the next one is: a `next` URL in the body
(`nextLink`, `@odata.nextLink` in Microsoft Graph), a `Link: <...>; rel="next"` header, or a continuation token.
A script that reads only the first page is the most common REST bug: the report is right in test and wrong in
production, where there is more data.
```powershell
$uri = 'https://api.example.com/v1/tickets?page=1'
$all = while ($uri) {
$page = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $uri -Headers $headers -TimeoutSec 15
$page.items                 # emit this page's items: the while loop's output is collected in $all
$uri = $page.next           # $null on the last page ends the loop
`-FollowRelLink` follows `Link` headers for you, but on PowerShell 7.6 it did not send the `Authorization` header
to the following pages against the lesson's API (it treats them like redirects), and many APIs put the next link
in the body anyway. The explicit loop works everywhere and is easy to log and limit.

steps.title: All the open tickets, every page
prompt: The ticket API at `http://127.0.0.1:8088/api/tickets` needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; your token is in
`~/.config/ops/api-token` (a file only you can read: look at its permissions with `ls -l ~/.config/ops`). Each page
Export **every ticket whose `status` is `open`**, from **all** pages, to `~/answers/open-tickets.csv` with the

checks.name: all open tickets from all pages
checks.fail: Not quite (see what the check found).

hints: Read the token without the trailing newline: `$token = (Get-Content ~/.config/ops/api-token -Raw).Trim()`. Then `$headers = @{ Authorization = "Bearer $token" }`.
Loop while there is a next page: `$uri = 'http://127.0.0.1:8088/api/tickets'; $all = while ($uri) { $p = Invoke-RestMethod $uri -Headers $headers; $p.items; $uri = $p.next }`.

`$all | Where-Object status -eq 'open' | Select-Object @{ n = 'Id'; e = { $_.id } }, @{ n = 'Title'; e = { $_.title } }, @{ n = 'Priority'; e = { $_.priority } } | Export-Csv ~/answers/open-tickets.csv`
solution: $all | Where-Object status -eq 'open' | Select-Object @{ n = 'Id'; e = { $_.id } }, @{ n = 'Title'; e = { $_.title } }, @{ n = 'Priority'; e = { $_.priority } } | Export-Csv -Path ~/answers/open-tickets.csv
explain: Collecting a loop's output with `$all = while (...) { ... }` is faster and cleaner than `$all += $item`, which copies
the whole array on every addition. For a real API, add a safety limit (`-and $n -lt 100`) and log each page, so a
server that keeps returning the same `next` cannot loop your job forever.

steps.prompt: A nightly report calls an API that sometimes answers `503 Service Unavailable` for a few seconds during deployments. What is the most robust change?
options: Wrap it in `try { } catch { }` and ignore the error
steps.explain: Built-in retries handle transient 5xx and 429 answers (and honour `Retry-After`), and the timeout stops a hung call from blocking the job. Ignoring the error produces an empty report; `-SkipHttpErrorCheck` just hands you the 503 to deal with yourself.

steps.title: Survive a flaky endpoint
prompt: `http://127.0.0.1:8088/api/flaky` answers **503** while the month-end report is being generated, then **200** with
the report. Try it once: `Invoke-RestMethod http://127.0.0.1:8088/api/flaky`.
Fetch the report **in one command that retries by itself** (at least 3 retries, 1 second apart), and save the

checks.name: the server saw the retries
checks.fail: The endpoint should have been called at least three times (two 503s, then the 200).

hints: `Get-Help Invoke-RestMethod -Parameter *Retry*` lists the two parameters you need.
explain: Retries are only safe for requests that can be repeated without harm: GET, PUT and DELETE are meant to be
*idempotent*; a POST that creates an order may create two. For those, the API needs an idempotency key header
(`Idempotency-Key: <guid>`), or the script must check before retrying.

steps.prompt: A health probe that never throws, never hangs, and reports the status code.
steps.explain: `-StatusCodeVariable` takes the variable's **name** without `$`, like `-ErrorVariable`. A connection error or a timeout still throws: `-SkipHttpErrorCheck` only covers HTTP error answers.
